article.title: Why Customer Frequency and Spending per Visit Tell Different Stories
article.why: 把消費額拆成頻率與單次金額，理解成長真正來源。
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
When customer spending rises, teams often celebrate the increase without asking how it happened. Yet total spending can grow for very different reasons. A customer may visit more often, spend more on each visit, or do both. Separating frequency from spending per visit makes the behavioral story much clearer.

At a simple level, total spending is approximately the number of transactions multiplied by average spending per transaction. Suppose a supermarket customer spent $1,200 last year and $1,440 this year. The 20 percent increase looks positive, but it does not tell us whether the customer became more frequent or simply bought more each time.

In one scenario, visits rise from 40 to 48 while spending per visit stays at $30. Growth comes entirely from frequency. This may suggest stronger habit, better convenience, or successful efforts to increase visit occasions. In another scenario, visits remain at 40 but spending per visit rises from $30 to $36. The same annual growth now reflects larger baskets, price changes, product mix, or inflation rather than more frequent engagement.

These stories can imply different actions. If frequency rises, a loyalty program may be strengthening routine behavior. The business might protect that habit through personalized offers or convenient services. If spending per visit rises but frequency falls, revenue may look healthy while customer engagement is weakening. The company may need to understand why visits are disappearing.

Analysts should also distinguish nominal price effects from behavioral change. Average basket value can increase because prices rose, even when customers buy the same or fewer items. If quantity data are available, basket size in units and price per unit provide another useful decomposition. Without that check, inflation can be mistaken for stronger customer demand.

Aggregation creates another complication. Imagine that heavy users leave while a small group of premium customers remains. Average spend per visit could rise because the customer mix changed, not because individual customers changed behavior. Comparing stable cohorts—customers observed in both periods—can help separate composition effects from within-customer change.

Frequency itself needs a clear definition. Are we counting transactions, shopping days, or months with at least one purchase? A customer who makes three transactions during one store visit may look unusually frequent if raw transaction count is used. The appropriate measure depends on the business question and data-generating process.

Seasonality also matters. Comparing six months that include December with six months that do not can distort both frequency and basket value. Use comparable periods, or model seasonal patterns explicitly. For stores, calendar effects such as holidays, weekends, and promotion periods can influence the two components differently.

A useful reporting table therefore shows total spend per customer, transaction frequency, average spend per transaction, and the percentage change in each. For important segments, add customer counts and user rates so that a shrinking population does not hide behind stronger averages.

The decomposition is especially valuable when designing customer ranks or incentives. If the goal is to encourage an additional visit, a threshold based only on annual spending may reward customers who already have high basket values without changing their frequency. A program can instead examine how far customers are from the next threshold in both money and realistic numbers of visits.

The main lesson is that revenue is an outcome, not a complete behavioral explanation. Two customers can produce the same annual spending through completely different patterns. By separating frequency and spending per visit, analysts can connect a change in revenue to a more specific hypothesis about customer behavior—and choose a response that fits the actual driver.

quiz.answer: It may reflect price increases or customer-mix changes rather than stronger individual behavior.
